claims.claim: BPE subword training starts from smaller symbols, repeatedly counts adjacent symbol pairs and merges the most frequent pair to form longer subword units.
claims.notes: Sennrich et al. adapt BPE to character sequences and word boundaries for neural machine translation.

claims.claim: Sennrich et al. use subword units to address rare and unseen words while balancing neural vocabulary size and sequence length.
claims.notes: The paper's original task is neural machine translation; later LLM tokenizers use related but not identical pipelines.

claims.claim: SentencePiece can train subword models directly from raw sentences without requiring external pre-tokenization and supports language-independent subword segmentation.
claims.notes: SentencePiece supports BPE and Unigram model types; its normalization and boundary behavior must still be configured.

claims.claim: The open-source tiktoken project describes itself as a fast BPE tokenizer for OpenAI models and exposes named encodings through get_encoding and encoding_for_model.
claims.notes: A tokenizer encoding name and special-token configuration must be pinned to reproduce exact token IDs.

claims.claim: The Hugging Face GPT-2 tokenizer implementation is byte-level BPE and treats spaces as part of tokens, so a word can tokenize differently at the beginning of a string and after a space.
claims.notes: The add_prefix_space option changes behavior and can differ from the tokenizer's pretraining convention.

claims.claim: The GPT-2 tokenizer configuration in tiktoken defines an explicit vocabulary size of 50,257 including the end-of-text special token ID.
claims.locator: gpt2() encoding definition; explicit_n_vocab and special_tokens
claims.notes: This is a specific encoding configuration, not a universal vocabulary-size recommendation.

claims.claim: A reproducible tokenizer requires more than a vocabulary list: pre-tokenization, normalization, byte mapping, merge ranks, special tokens and serialization behavior affect output IDs.
claims.locator: Encoding definitions and public tokenizer implementation; engineering synthesis
claims.notes: The exact components differ by tokenizer family; do not assume GPT-2, SentencePiece and Unigram share one pipeline.

claims.claim: Cross-language bytes-per-token is not a suitable standalone compression comparison because equivalent content in different languages can have different byte premiums; the NeurIPS 2025 study instead measures corpus token counts on parallel texts.
claims.notes: The study uses parallel FLORES text and corpus token count (CTC), optionally normalized by a reference language. Bytes/token remains useful for within-language engineering measurements.
